title: Allow defining a function globally within a local scope
author: Oxicid

text: What problem, specifically, are you trying to work around? I don’t see why bar needs to be a global function if it depends on a local variable. I don’t see a compelling reason to add dynamic scoping to Python.
author: chepner

text:
This works:
g_bar = None

def foo():
    global g_bar
    x = 12
    def bar():
        print(x)
    bar()
    g_bar = bar

foo()
g_bar()
author: barry-scott

text:
Oxicid:

Sometimes linters complain about shadowed names, forcing you to rename variables or move local functions to the global scope.


Is there a reason you can’t just turn off the linter rule and work to your own code style?
I shadow names like hash, dir and id in Python all the time, since I often have more important things that want to use those names, and if I want to use both (usually with hash) I’ll just write something like _hash = hash near the top of the file.
author: rrolls

text:
The global keyword is needed for bar to ensure that local variables from foo are not accidentally used. Usually, this is handled by creating a separate function outside the local scope, but this can clutter the namespace of both the class and the function.
In short, the global keyword guarantees that local variables from the outer function are not used.
author: Oxicid

text: Yes, I also use a workaround by appending an underscore to the name (e.g. var_). This is actually what led me to come up with this proposal, which would help avoid cluttering variable names.
author: Oxicid

text:
You don’t even need to fiddle around with multiple names or pre-define the global:
def foo():
    global g_bar
    x = 12
    def g_bar():
        print(x)
    g_bar()

foo()
g_bar()

text:
This decorator handles the task quite nicely. Python never ceases to amaze me! 
def assert_no_freevars(func):
    assert not func.__closure__

It’s a shame that PyCharm still complains, but that’s a separate issue.

author: Oxicid

text:
Your decorator should also return the original function. Otherwise the check will work, but the function won’t as the decorator returns None so the function is replaced by None.
def assert_no_freevars(func):
    assert not func.__closure__

def assert_no_freevars_return(func):
    assert not func.__closure__
    return func

def outer():
    @assert_no_freevars_return
    def inner1():
        print("This function still works")
    @assert_no_freevars
    def inner2():
        print("This function is replaced by None")
    print(inner1, inner2)
    inner1()
    inner2()

outer()

<function outer.<locals>.inner1 at 0x106d92cf0> None
This function still works
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<python-input-0>", line 19, in <module>
    outer()
    ~~~~~^^
  File "<python-input-0>", line 17, in outer
    inner2()
    ~~~~~~^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable

It might also be worth noting that if the function doesn’t use any nonlocals defining it in the global scope once is faster as the inner function isn’t being rebuilt on every outer function call.
